title: Joe Rodas as player and person
summary: Jones and Allen describe Rodas as a unique stylist, intelligent and earthy, who taught Jones much and declined through drinking and heart trouble.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Yeah, well, he's one of those people that I heard people talk about. And of course, I always thought of him as a comedian, a clown, who flew around with the trombone and play stuff. And so often I heard him do, he was very, very funny. I'm not belittling him.

He was a good showman. And Joe's biggest trouble was, I guess, in getting any recognition for his playing, was that he didn't play like anybody else. He was a stylist. If you listen to Joe Rodas play, you'd say, hey, that's Joe Rodas. You don't say, hey, that's Joe Rodas. He sounds a little bit like, see, because nobody could put a handle on him. He just, that's the way he played. Very unique player. But he played very well. And he got the, he knew what the trombone player was supposed to do in a band and did it, but his own way.
Nobody paid me into it. He's a clown. To me, he was funnier than Pete or George. I think of them

as being three clowns. Well, Pete was very backward and not very articulate and still isn't. I mean, like, you know, he's got a routine, you know, his little lines that he uses in his show and it comes across very well. But he's not a very articulate person. But Rodas was. Rodas was a very intelligent person. Well read and he spoke French. I mean, like a native, fluently. Yeah. And was familiar with classical literature, both musical and literature, you know. But he

I really didn't know him that well. He was a very warm person. Yeah. Very loving person. Yeah. And and open and giving. He was very generous with himself. Mm-hmm. And taught me an awful lot. And had patience with me. And he did a world of good for me. I watched him drink himself and I didn't see Joe for maybe two years after I moved up to Philadelphia. And he came up there to play with the band for a while. And had just deteriorated to the point where he could not, he just couldn't play anymore. He couldn't get that happy medium between being sober and just the buzz that he wanted. There was no in between. He was either sober or he was uncontrollably drunk. And when he, he was one of those guys that could not play when he had too much to drink. Could not play. Just lost all control. Mm-hmm. Well, I remember him having a heart attack and going in back to hospital. And I guess he came back and played some more after that. Well, the first heart attack he had, yeah, it was a Yeah, it was before I joined the band. Not too, maybe a year or so, I believe. Which would have to be about 1951, 1952. And then I believe he did have another one after that. But after the band had broken up. He was, his health was going on him after that. But the doctors told him he probably would never be active again, much less play. And he just made lives out of him. He went down swinging. He was going to swing at you. But he was grossly overweight. He was one of those kind of guys that would sit down and eat three po' boys and then go looking for something to chase him with. Like a couple dozen hot tamales from manuals on Kalten and Canal. Just a wonderful eater. Yeah, it's a miracle. Yeah, it's a miracle. His stomach didn't fall out. That too, yeah. And liver.
